lesson.title: How a Switch Learns Where Everyone Lives
lesson.summary: A learning switch builds its MAC address table automatically, by watching the source address of every frame it sees, so it never needs to be manually configured with a map of the network. This self learning algorithm is the specific mechanism behind the forwarding behavior introduced in the switch and bridge chapters.
lesson.body:
The previous two chapters described bridges and switches deciding whether to forward or filter a frame based on a table of MAC addresses and ports, but skipped over an important question: where does that table come from? Nobody sits down and types in a list of which device lives behind which port. Instead, a modern switch builds this table entirely on its own, through a process called learning, and it does so using nothing more than the frames already flowing through it.

The learning algorithm relies on one simple insight: whoever sent a frame must be reachable through the port that frame arrived on. So for every single frame the switch receives, regardless of its destination, the switch first looks at the source MAC address and records, or refreshes, an entry in its table mapping that source address to the incoming port. Only after updating this record does the switch turn to the actual forwarding decision. It looks up the frame's destination MAC address in the table. If there is a matching entry and that entry points to a different port than the one the frame arrived on, the switch forwards the frame out that one port only. If the destination happens to map to the same port the frame came in on, the switch drops it, since the intended recipient is already reachable directly from that segment. And if the destination address has no entry at all yet, the switch floods the frame out every other port, the same fallback behavior described for bridges when a destination is unknown.

Table entries do not last forever. Each one carries an aging timer, and if the switch does not see any further traffic from a given MAC address within that window, commonly on the order of a few minutes, it removes the entry. This matters because devices get unplugged, moved to different ports, or replaced with new hardware carrying a different address, and without aging a switch could keep forwarding frames toward a port where the intended device no longer exists.

Trace through a switch immediately after it powers on, with an empty table and three PCs, A, B, and C, attached to ports 1, 2, and 3. PC A sends its first frame, addressed to PC C. The switch has no entries at all, so it learns A lives at port 1, then checks for C's address, finds nothing, and floods the frame out ports 2 and 3. PC C's network card recognizes the destination address as its own and accepts the frame; PC B's card ignores it. Now suppose C replies to A. The switch learns that C lives at port 3, looks up A's address, and this time finds a match: port 1. It forwards C's reply out port 1 alone, with no flooding this time, because the table now has what it needs. Within just two frames, the switch has learned enough to stop guessing.

This is what makes a learning switch effectively plug and play: no administrator has to configure a single address, and the table only ever grows entries for devices that are actually communicating, which keeps it efficient even on a large network. It is also self correcting: if a laptop is unplugged from port 1 and later plugged into port 4, the switch simply learns the new mapping the next time that laptop sends a frame, while the stale port 1 entry quietly ages out. The elegance of this algorithm, address discovery entirely as a byproduct of normal traffic, is one of the reasons switched Ethernet scaled so well from small offices to enormous campus networks.
